headline: Massachusetts hiker dies on West Rattlesnake Mountain in Holderness
dek: Richard Chateauneuf, 64, was found unconscious about three-quarters of a mile from the trailhead Saturday. Other hikers and first responders attempted CPR, but he could not be revived.
body: A 64-year-old Massachusetts man died Saturday after he was found unconscious on the Old Bridle Path at West Rattlesnake Mountain in Holderness, New Hampshire, according to the [New Hampshire Fish and Game Department](https://nhfishgame.com/2026/10/05/deceased-hiker-on-old-bridle-path-on-west-rattlesnake-mountain/). Richard Chateauneuf of Tyngsboro was about three-quarters of a mile from the trailhead when other hikers found him and began administering CPR, the department said.

The call came at 11:22 a.m. on Oct. 3, the agency said. Holderness Fire-Rescue, Center Harbor Fire-Rescue, Sandwich Fire-Rescue, Plymouth Ambulance and Fish and Game conservation officers responded to the trail. First responders continued efforts to revive Chateauneuf, but he could not be revived. His body was carried back to the trailhead, according to the official account.

Independent reports from [NBC Boston](https://www.nbcboston.com/news/local/massachusetts-man-dies-while-hiking-in-nhs-lakes-region/4025511/) and [WMUR](https://www.wmur.com/article/hiker-dies-holderness-trail/74008418) matched the department's account of the response and identified Chateauneuf as a Tyngsboro resident. Neither report described a cause of death, and Fish and Game said no additional information was available. The circumstances should therefore be understood as an unexplained medical emergency, not as a reported fall, weather incident or trail accident.

West Rattlesnake Mountain is in New Hampshire's Lakes Region, near the town of Holderness. [CBS Boston](https://www.cbsnews.com/boston/news/hiker-dies-west-rattlesnake-mountain-new-hampshire/) reported that the Old Bridle Path is a popular 1.8-mile route with about 396 feet of elevation gain that typically takes roughly an hour and a half. Distance from a road still matters when a hiker needs urgent medical care: the location reported by officials, less than a mile from the trailhead, shows why a medical crisis on a modest outing can require a coordinated response rather than a routine ambulance call.

The response depended on both public agencies and people already on the trail. Hikers who found Chateauneuf called for help and started CPR before emergency crews arrived. Fish and Game said the incident brought together local fire and rescue departments, an ambulance service and state conservation officers, with the patient then carried to the trailhead for removal from the mountain.

The department used the release to renew its broader hiking-safety message. New Hampshire Fish and Game describes itself as a self-funded agency that relies heavily on volunteer rescue groups for wilderness search-and-rescue work. It encourages hikers to prepare with the ten essentials: a map and compass, warm clothing, extra food and water, a headlamp, fire starter, a first-aid kit, a whistle, rain and wind protection, and a knife. The list appears in the department's current release about the Holderness response.

Fish and Game also promotes the voluntary [Hike Safe card](https://gc.nh.gov/rules/state_agencies/fis1100.html), which supports the state's search-and-rescue fund. The card is not a substitute for preparation or a guarantee that a hiker will avoid responsibility for a response; state rules address circumstances involving negligence or reckless conduct. The department's message after Saturday's death was practical: plan the route, account for changing conditions and carry equipment that can help until rescuers arrive.

No investigation or medical finding explaining Chateauneuf's death was announced in the official release. For now, the confirmed facts are the location, response time, identity, rescue effort and death. The incident is a reminder for residents and visitors using Holderness trails that even a familiar, relatively short hike can become a medical emergency far enough from a road to test both a hiker's preparation and the region's rescue network.
location: West Rattlesnake Mountain, Holderness, New Hampshire
author: NorthEast News Desk
